raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male presented with the complaints of fever with chills and rigor accompanied with severe headache, vomiting, convulsions, and altered sensorium for 6 days. He had no history of recreational drug use, diabetes, and hypertension. He also did not reveal any history suggestive of renal parenchymal disease or vasculitis.
On examination, he was comatose, febrile (102 F), pulse - 130/min, and BP - 140/70 mm Hg. Neurological examination revealed a comatose patient with bilateral constricted sluggish-reacting pupils without other cranial nerve deficits. Plantar response was bilaterally extensor. There was decerebrate posturing and neck rigidity was mild. Cardiovascular examination revealed no abnormality of peripheral pulses, bruits or cardiomegaly. Respiratory and abdominal examination revealed no abnormality.
Blood counts revealed a normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin - 9.7 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume - 90 fl), ESR - 28 mm/h, and platelet count of 75,000/cu.mm. Thick and thin blood smears were prepared and it revealed ring forms and gametocytes of P. falciparum and immunochromatographic test for PfHRP-2 based assay (ICT, Access Bio. Inc., NJ, USA) was strongly positive. Biochemical investigations - LFTs, renal function tests, and serum electrolytes were within the normal limits. No abnormality was found on urine examination with respect to proteinuria, red blood cells, white blood cells or casts. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for human immunodeficiency virus was negative.
A clinical diagnosis of cerebral malaria caused by P. falciparum was established, and the patient was started on intravenous artesunate therapy. Following a lack of improvement in sensorium despite 3 days of antimalarial treatment, a non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan brain was advised, which surprisingly revealed subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) [Figure 1]. A coagulation screen was found to be within normal range. Prothrombin time-international normalized ratio was 1.3 and activated partial thromboplastin time was 32 s. Fibrin degradation products by D-dimer were negative. A magnetic resonance angiography was carried out, which revealed no arterio-venous malformation or aneurysm. Anti-nuclear antibody titers were found to be negative by standard method. There was no family history of sickle cell anemia, and a sickling test on peripheral blood smear using sodium metabisulfite was negative.
The patient had a stormy clinical course and ultimately died 3 days later in spite of aggressive treatment with intravenous artesunate and supporting ventilator measures.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with a 6-day history of high fever with chills, severe headache, vomiting, generalized convulsions, and progressive coma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced high fever with chills and rigors, severe headache, and vomiting starting 6 days prior to presentation. Over the preceding 24-48 hours, he developed generalized seizures and unresponsiveness. On admission, he was comatose with decerebrate posturing and mild nuchal rigidity. Despite aggressive antimalarial treatment and supportive intensive care, his neurological status failed to improve over 3 days, prompting neuroimaging.
subjective.past_medical_history: Non-diabetic, non-hypertensive. Denied history of recreational drug use, renal parenchymal disease, vascular disorders, or prior seizures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, severe headache, vomiting, generalized convulsions, and coma. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 102 F, heart rate: 130 beats/min, blood pressure: 140/70 mmHg. Neurological: Deeply comatose, decerebrate posturing; pupils bilaterally constricted with sluggish light reaction; mild neck rigidity present; bilateral extensor plantar responses. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL, MCV: 90 fL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 28 mm/h, platelet count: 75,000/cu.mm. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and serum electrolytes: Within normal limits. Urinalysis: Normal without proteinuria, hematuria, pyuria, or casts. Coagulation screen: Prothrombin time-INR: 1.3, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT): 32 seconds, D-dimer / fibrin degradation products: Negative. HIV ELISA: Negative. Antinuclear antibody (ANA): Negative. Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite): Negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast brain CT scan: Demonstrated acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in basal cisterns and sulcal spaces. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of brain: No detectable intracranial aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation (AVM).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute spontaneous non-aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), decerebrate posturing, and fatal cerebral dysfunction.
Diagnostic confirmation: Thick and thin blood smears demonstrated ring forms and gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum; immunochromatographic test for PfHRP-2 was strongly positive. Structural vascular lesions (aneurysm, AVM), systemic vasculitis, sickle cell trait/disease, and systemic coagulopathy were ruled out by MRA, ANA, sickling test, and normal coagulation parameters.
Plan & Outcome: Managed in the intensive care unit with endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and intravenous artesunate therapy. Despite aggressive supportive care and antiparasitic therapy, the patient suffered progressive neurological devastation secondary to massive subarachnoid hemorrhage and died 3 days following neuroimaging.
